# The model

A count [outcome](model-validation.qmd#def-outcome-vector),
such as the number of bike rentals in an hour,
is not well described by a [normal distribution](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-normal)
when the counts are small,
since the normal distribution puts [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) below zero,
and a count is never below zero.
A [Poisson regression model](poisson-regression.qmd#def-poisson-regression) takes the [event rate](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/distributions.html#def-event-rate)
to be the [exponential function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-exponential-function) of a [linear function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-linear-function) of the [covariates](model-validation.qmd#def-covariate).

# Lab: Poisson regression on bike rentals {#sec-bikeshare-lab}

```{r}
#| include: false
bikeshare_raw <- readr::read_csv("data/bikeshare.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bikeshare_n <- nrow(bikeshare_raw)
```

Hourly counts of bikes rented in a bike-sharing program in Washington, D.C.,
on `r bikeshare_n` hours make up the `Bikeshare` data [@james2021islr2e, Section 4.6.2].
The data are in [`data/bikeshare.csv`](data/bikeshare.csv), one line per hour,
copied from the book's `ISLR2` R package.
The exercises use these variables:

- `bikers`: the [outcome](model-validation.qmd#def-outcome-vector), the number of bikes rented in that hour.
- `temp`: the temperature, scaled to run from $0$ to $1$.
- `workingday`: `1` on a working day and `0` otherwise.
- `weathersit`: the weather, one of `clear`, `cloudy/misty`, `light rain/snow`, and `heavy rain/snow`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### R

```{r}
#| code-fold: show
# The first rows of the four columns that the exercises use.
bikeshare_raw |>
  dplyr::select(bikers, temp, workingday, weathersit) |>
  head()
```

##### Python

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
import pandas as pd

# The first rows of the four columns that the exercises use.
bikeshare_raw = pd.read_csv("data/bikeshare.csv")
bikeshare_raw[["bikers", "temp", "workingday", "weathersit"]].head(6)
```

:::

The exercises follow the [Poisson regression](poisson-regression.qmd#def-poisson-regression) part of the book's Chapter 4 lab [@james2021islr2e, Section 4.7.7].
Each solution shows the code in R and in Python.
